extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social institutions, literature, and intellectual history
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-level analytical essay examining how democratic conditions and social institutions shape literary, artistic, and intellectual production and the conditions that foster or hinder creative intellectual power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration for literary or scientific eminence
rubrics_metrics.description: An admiration for literary or scientific eminence, an enthusiasm for anything that can be called genius, with undue eagerness to discover it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the characteristic tendencies of the people at large; signals a cultural predisposition to hunt for 'genius' which can skew evaluation and taste by overvaluing apparent brilliance rather than tested merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion for novelties
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also listed among popular tendencies; implies that taste and demand may favour what is new over what is durable or deeply crafted, affecting both production and reception of literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual impatience and desire for quick results
rubrics_metrics.description: An intellectual impatience, and desire for quick and patent results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This impatience encourages work that yields fast, obvious effects rather than patiently developed, subtle, or technically finished creations; the author links this tendency to democratic/popular conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-valuing the judgments of the multitude
rubrics_metrics.description: An over-valuing of the judgments of the multitude; a disposition to judge by newspaper success work which has not been produced with a view to such success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that equating newspaper/popular success with quality is a poor evaluative standard; producers who seek broad popular approval may abandon refinements needed for higher literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking bigness for greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency to mistake bigness for greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions against conflating scale, publicity or sheer size of audience with intrinsic artistic or intellectual merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-confidence/self-complacency that prevents testing of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy produces self-confidence and self-complacency, national and personal, which stimulates thought but prevents the thought that is produced from being subjected to proper tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cultural self-assurance may encourage production but inhibit critical scrutiny and rigorous testing, thereby lowering the standard of what is produced or accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-judgment is a poor artistic standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgment of the masses is a poor standard for the thinker or the artist to set before him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit normative claim: artists and thinkers should not use popular taste as their primary standard; doing so narrows view, debases style, and leads to avoidance of novelty or subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to the mass—preserve refinements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the mass rules, a writer cannot but think of the mass, and if refinements are not appreciated he will eschew them, making himself... intelligible to the common mind, and seeking to attract by broad, perhaps coarsely broad, effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for producers: resist tailoring style and substance to the lowest-common-denominator reader, because it leads to coarseness and loss of refinement; examples include trading lasting literature for fashionable sketches or sensational crime stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating democratic influence requires a general, majority-running quality
rubrics_metrics.description: To show democracy's influence on literature one must demonstrate a general quality running through the majority of writers — a quality which is at once recognized as racy of the soil and which can be traced back to the democratic element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criterion for attributing cause: isolated instances or a few individual writers are insufficient evidence; one must identify an attribute widespread among the body of writers and plausibly linked to democratic conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population size does not correlate with genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers have nothing to do with the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical claim against simple numeric explanations: a large population does not necessarily produce more geniuses or increase the average of top creative talent; therefore evaluations should not presume quantity implies quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for tranquillity, time, and concentrated meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tranquillity and repose are necessary to men of creative power; he must have time to meditate, to pause, to set his creation aside and return with fresh eyes; he must be able to concentrate the whole force of his reason or imagination on one subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive criterion for producing high literary/artistic/philosophic work: uninterrupted time, ability to reflect deeply and return to work after intervals are essential conditions for original and well-finished creations. Examples: Dante, Hegel, Bunyan, Cervantes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unrestfulness and ceaseless external impressions hinder deep work
rubrics_metrics.description: The unrestfulness, ceaseless stir and constant presence of newspapers and external impressions render life exciting but chase away opportunities for repose and meditation which art and philosophy need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual diagnosis: societies or times with perpetual distraction and rapid news cycles make it harder for creators to achieve the concentrated, slow work required for higher literature; this is offered as an explanation for relative scarcity of sustained creative production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural temperament favoring quick practicality reduces patient craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of mind which American conditions have evolved is quick, vigorous, practical, versatile; but it is unfavourable to the natural germination and slow ripening of large and luminous ideas; it wants the patience that will spend weeks or months on bringing details to an exquisite perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative claim about national/cultural dispositions: energetic practicality produces many virtues but tends to undermine long, patient processes needed for certain high forms of literature and art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance of material/practical interests diverts talent from higher arts and science
rubrics_metrics.description: The predominance of material and practical interests has turned men's thoughts into channels unfavourable to the growth of the higher and more solid kinds of literature; attractions of practical life (railways, finance, commerce, inventions) have absorbed many strenuous talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains a structural cause: economic and practical priorities in a society can lower supply of talent available for pure science, philosophy, or high literature; this is both an observation and an implicit evaluative standard when assessing national creative output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of historic monuments and associations reduces imaginative stimulus
rubrics_metrics.description: In a new country one whole set of objects which appeal to the imagination are absent — no castles gray with age; no solemn cathedrals... few spots or edifices consecrated by memories of famous men or deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that physical/historical environment matters: the lack of venerable sites and long historical associations lessens the imaginative resources that nurture certain kinds of literary and artistic inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on foreign (English) literature and cheap reprints discourages native production
rubrics_metrics.description: Many books which America might produce are not produced because qualified men know there are already English books on the same subject; the profusion of cheap reprints (many flimsy novels) drove better books out of the market and tended to vulgarize taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market and cultural dependency criterion: widespread consumption of imported or cheap popular literature can depress native authorship, lower public taste, and create an atmosphere unfavourable to the growth of higher literature; cited as both economic and cultural mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits of popular government can open careers to talent (positive effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The habits of popular government which open a career to talent in public life, open it in literature also: a pure clear voice with an unwonted message may at first fail but once heard will probably be judged on its own merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced/positive criterion: democratic openness can allow talent to succeed without needing factional backing; this is a countervailing factor that can improve meritocratic access for literary voices.
